Hot aisle and cold aisle containment — the most practical improvement in Data Center cooling efficiency. Hot/Cold Aisle Containment — Data Center cooling improvement guide. 1px solid rgba(37,99,235,0.08) Containment physically separates cool air and hot air — so that the two do not mix. This dramatically improves cooling efficiency. The problem without containment The PAC/CRAC delivers cool air. Before the hot air comes back, it mixes with the cool air. The PAC has to work twice as hard — air that was already cooled got warm again. Cold aisle containment (CAC) An enclosure is installed over the top and ends of the cold aisle. Cool air is captured there. Only the server intakes pull in the cool air. Hot air stays separate. Hot aisle containment (HAC) An enclosure over the top and ends of the hot aisle. Hot air is captured. It returns directly to the PAC/CRAC or through a chimney. Cool air stays in the room. How much improvement Containment can improve cooling efficiency by 30-50%. Fewer cooling units or higher setpoints for the same cooling load — significant energy savings. Blanking panels Blanking panels are also essential with containment — block the empty rack spaces. So warm air does not come in from the front. Small thing, big impact.

faqs.q: Which is better, CAC or HAC?
faqs.a: Both are effective. HAC generally gives better cooling efficiency — hot air is directly captured and returned, and the room

faqs.q: Can the temperature setpoint be raised after containment?
faqs.a: Yes — this is a major benefit. Without containment, the cold aisle needs 18-20°C because mixing happens. After containment, the cold aisle can be 24-26°C — server inlet still within spec. Higher setpoint = the PAC/CRAC works less = energy savings.

faqs.q: How does containment work with fire suppression?
faqs.a: This is a real concern. In HAC the hot aisle is enclosed. The fire suppression agent must distribute properly in this enclosed space. FM200 or Novec — validate the design with an engineer. In some facilities the containment doors open automatically on a fire signal.

faqs.q: Why are blanking panels important with containment?
faqs.a: Blanking panels seal the empty rack spaces. Without blanking panels, hot exhaust air can come back through the rack from the front — hot/cold mixing. Even with containment, blanking panels are essential — they ensure a perfect seal.

faqs.q: How is containment implemented on a raised floor?
faqs.a: Downflow PAC/CRAC is used with a raised floor. The cold aisle has perforated tiles — cool air comes from here. In cold aisle containment: seal the top and ends of the cold aisle. Only the server intakes pull in the cool air — perfect separation.

faqs.q: Is it possible to retrofit containment in an existing data center?
faqs.a: Yes — this is common practice. Retrofit containment systems are available — modular panels that fit on existing infrastructure. Planning is essential: power paths, cable management, fire suppression, emergency access. ROI is typically 1-3 years from energy savings.

headings: How Cooling Tower Works in a Data Center
A cooling tower is a heat rejection device that releases the chiller
On the building roof or at ground level (outside). Connected to the chiller
cooling-tower.bodyText: 🏭 QUICK SUMMARY — 2 MINUTE READ Engineer's Tip Why This Matters In A Data Center On The Data Center Map KEY TAKEAWAYS The chiller absorbs the data center's heat. But this heat has to go somewhere — permanently outside. How does the chiller remove this heat? Through the cooling tower. Cooling tower = the chiller's heat dumping station. It is a simple device — but without it a water-cooled chiller plant cannot run. And without a cooling tower, a large data center's cooling will fail. Cooling towers — typically on the data center building's roof or on the ground outside. These towers reject heat into the atmosphere. What Is a Cooling Tower? A cooling tower is a heat rejection device. It cools hot water — through the evaporative cooling process — and releases the heat into the atmosphere. Daily life analogy: In summer you sweat. The sweat evaporates. You feel cool. Same principle — in a cooling tower water evaporates and heat goes out. In a data center the cooling tower works specifically with the chiller plant The chiller's condenser side gets hot — when the refrigerant rejects heat. This heat has to be removed somewhere. The cooling tower does this job. Why Is Cooling Tower Needed? In the chiller refrigeration cycle, heat is transferred at two places: Evaporator side: Heat is absorbed from the chilled water → the data center gets cooled ✓ Condenser side: This heat has to be rejected somewhere → COOLING TOWER ✓ If the condenser side heat is not rejected, the chiller will be overloaded. High pressure trip. Cooling stops. Energy balance: The heat the cooling tower has to reject = the data center's IT heat + the chiller's own power consumption. Example: 1000 kW data center heat + 200 kW chiller power = 1200 kW the cooling tower has to reject. The water-cooled chiller + cooling tower combination achieves a COP of 4-7 in data center cooling. An air-cooled chiller's COP is 2.5-4. This means: using a cooling tower takes 30-40% less electricity for the same cooling. In a large data center this can be monthly savings of lakhs of rupees. Working Principle Evaporative cooling — this is the core principle of the cooling tower. Simple experiment: Put water on a cloth. The water evaporates. The cloth becomes cool. Why? Evaporation needs energy — this energy comes from the heat of the surrounding water. Result: the water becomes cool. Step by Step Process Step 1 — Hot water in: Hot water (35-40°C) from the chiller condenser enters the cooling tower. The distribution header distributes this water evenly. Step 2 — Fill media: The hot water trickles over the fill media (packing/fill — structured sheets of plastic or wood). The fill maximizes surface area — more surface = more evaporation. Step 3 — Airflow: The cooling tower fan draws atmospheric air. The air passes through the fill media — it comes into contact with the water. Step 4 — Evaporation: Some water (1-2%) evaporates. This evaporation absorbs the heat of the remaining water. Result: the remaining water becomes cool. Step 5 — Cold water: Cool water (28-32°C) collects in the basin. Condenser water pumps pump this cold water to the chiller's condenser. Cycle repeats. Understand this important point: the chilled water loop (blue) and the condenser water loop (red/yellow) are SEPARATE. They never mix. The chiller works as a heat exchanger between them. Chilled water goes only to the CRAH. Condenser water circulates only in the cooling tower and the chiller condenser. Main Components 1. Fill Media (Packing) For distributing water — it maximizes surface area. Structured sheets of PVC plastic or treated wood. Counter-flow fill: water down, air up. Cross-flow fill: water down, air horizontal. It draws air into the tower. Axial (propeller type) or centrifugal. VFD controlled — vary the speed, save energy. Induced draft (fan on top) or forced draft (fan at the bottom). 3. Drift Eliminators 4. Water Distribution System From the hot water inlet to the header. Nozzles or gravity distribution — distributes water evenly over the fill media. Proper distribution = even cooling = efficient operation. The bottom section of the tower. Cool water collects here. Float valve — controls the water level. Makeup water supply — the water lost to evaporation is supplied here. Blowdown outlet — to remove concentrated minerals. 6. Makeup Water System It compensates for the water lost to evaporation. Float valve based automatic control. Treated water — controlling minerals is essential. 7. Chemical Dosing System Scale inhibitor, corrosion inhibitor, biocide, pH control — dosed regularly. This is the most important maintenance item — also for Legionella prevention. How Cooling Tower Works in a Data Center Understand the full loop: Servers → warm air → CRAH → warm chilled water → chiller evaporator → chiller condenser → hot condenser water → cooling tower → heat rejected to atmosphere. The cooling tower is the final heat rejection point. Without a cooling tower, where will the heat go? Nowhere — the system will fail. Remember the condenser water temperatures: Supply to chiller (CDWS) = 28-32°C, Return from chiller (CDWR) = 35-40°C. Delta T = 5-8°C. If the CDW temperature is higher, chiller efficiency drops and condenser pressure goes high. The cooling tower must work properly — chiller performance depends on it directly. Types of Cooling Towers By Airflow Direction Counter-Flow: Air flows up, water down. Maximum contact — efficient. Compact design. Most common in data centers. Air flows horizontally. Water down. Larger footprint. Easier maintenance — better fill access. Some large installations. Induced Draft: Fan on top — pulls air upward. Most common. Better air distribution. Discharge air passes through the fan — less splash back. Forced Draft: Fan at the bottom or side — pushes air. Icing risk in cold climates. Less common. By Construction Factory-Assembled (Package): The complete unit is built in the factory; install it on site. Small to medium — up to 1000 TR. Quick installation. Common for data centers. Field-Erected: Large cooling towers — built on site. High capacity. In hyperscale facilities. High efficiency: Evaporative cooling — 30-40% more efficient than air-cooled Lower condenser water temperature: 28-32°C vs air-cooled 35-45°C — chiller better COP Multiple cell towers — operate cells according to load VFD energy savings: Variable fan speed = significant energy reduction Wet bulb dependent: Consider humidity in India — but still better than air-cooled Disadvantages Water consumption: Evaporation + blowdown = significant water use Legionella risk: Warm water environment — regular treatment mandatory Water treatment cost: Chemicals, testing, management — ongoing cost Scaling and fouling: Minerals concentrate — scale deposits on the fill and heat exchangers Maintenance complexity: Regular cleaning, basin, fill, drift eliminators Wet bulb dependency: Effectiveness reduces at high humidity Freeze risk: In cold climates — special precautions in winter Real Data Center Example 10 MW data center, Mumbai. Chiller plant: 4 × 2500 kW water-cooled centrifugal chillers. Cooling tower design: 4 cooling towers (one per chiller) × 3000 kW rejection capacity each. N+1 cells within each tower — modular design. Condenser water: Supply 28°C (to chiller), Return 35°C (from chiller). Water treatment: Automatic chemical dosing system. Weekly water quality testing. Legionella monitoring — monthly testing. All towers with VFD — fan speed adjusts with load and ambient temperature. Estimated 40% fan energy savings vs fixed speed. Common Faults High Condenser Water Temperature (CDWS High) Cause: Fan failure, dirty fill, high ambient wet bulb, low water flow. Impact: High chiller condenser pressure → efficiency drop → potential trip. Action: Fan status check, fill inspect, flow verify. Fan Motor Failure Cause: Motor burnout, bearing failure, overload. Impact: Reduced cooling capacity — adjacent cell load increases. Action: Replace with a spare motor, redistribute the load. Basin Low Water Level Cause: Makeup water failure, float valve stuck, excess blowdown. Impact: Pump cavitation, reduced flow. Action: Makeup water supply check, float valve inspect. Scale Deposits on Fill Cause: Poor water treatment, high TDS, insufficient blowdown. Impact: Reduced airflow through fill, poor heat transfer. Action: Chemical cleaning, blowdown increase, water treatment review. Drift Eliminator Damage Cause: Physical damage, UV degradation, improper cleaning. Impact: Water drift — Legionella risk, neighbor complaints, water waste. Action: Inspect visually, replace damaged sections. Preventive Maintenance Water quality test — pH, TDS, hardness, inhibitor levels Chemical dosing check — levels adequate Basin visual inspect — debris, algae Fan operation check Full water quality analysis Legionella monitoring (culture test) Fan vibration check Clean the basin Inspect the distribution system — check for clogged nozzles Drift eliminator condition check Full tower shutdown and cleaning Fill inspection — replace if fouled Basin complete clean Fan blade inspection Motor insulation test Thermal performance test — actual vs design capacity Daily Inspection Checklist ✓ Condenser water supply temperature (target 28-32°C) ✓ Condenser water return temperature (target 35-40°C) ✓ All fan status — running, speed ✓ Basin water level — adequate ✓ Makeup water supply — working ✓ Unusual noise or vibration ✓ Chemical dosing system — operating ✓ BMS alarms ✓ Visual: debris, bird nests, visible damage ✓ Make a log entry Monthly Checklist ✓ Water quality test — pH, TDS, Langelier Saturation Index ✓ Legionella culture test — from a lab ✓ Chemical stock check — adequate supply ✓ Clean the basin — sediment, algae ✓ Fan vibration measurement ✓ Distribution nozzles — clog check ✓ Drift eliminator visual check ✓ Verify the blowdown rate ✓ Makeup water meter reading Safety Precautions Legionella prevention: Most critical. Proper biocide treatment, temperature management, regular testing. Deaths can happen if it is neglected. Working at height: Towers on the roof — full fall protection, anchor points, training Rotating equipment: Fan blades — LOTO before any access near fans Water hazard: Wet surfaces — slip hazard. Non-slip footwear. Chemical handling: Biocide, acid — PPE mandatory, COSHH assessment Motor maintenance — LOTO mandatory Confined space: Tower basin access — confined space permit Fan noise — hearing protection near operating towers Interview Questions Q1: What is the principle of a cooling tower? Evaporative cooling. Hot water trickles through the fill media. The fan draws atmospheric air. Some water evaporates — this evaporation absorbs the heat of the remaining water. Result: cold water returns. The heat goes into the atmosphere. Q2: Why are the condenser water loop and the chilled water loop separate? Chilled water loop = clean, treated, closed loop — it goes to the CRAH. Condenser water loop = open loop, exposed in the cooling tower, contamination from the atmosphere is possible. If they mix, the chilled water will be contaminated — CRAH coils will foul and water quality will degrade. The chiller works as a heat exchanger between the two — there is no mixing. Q3: What is Legionella and why is it a concern in a cooling tower? Legionella pneumophila is a bacteria that causes Legionnaires' disease — a serious respiratory illness. The warm (25-45°C) standing water of a cooling tower is a perfect breeding environment. Infected water droplets can go into the atmosphere through drift — inhaling them causes infection. Prevention: regular biocide treatment, proper temperature control, regular cleaning, monthly Legionella testing. Q4: What is approach temperature? Approach = Cooling tower leaving water temperature - Wet bulb temperature of ambient air. Smaller approach = better tower performance. Typical: 3-5°C. It cannot go below the wet bulb temperature (thermodynamic limit). High humidity = high wet bulb = limited cooling possible — this is the fundamental limitation of a cooling tower. Check the speed Ambient wet bulb temperature high? → The approach may be at the design limit Fill fouled? → Inspect and clean Water distribution blocked? → Check the nozzles Start additional tower cells if available Legionella detected in test Immediately call a qualified water treatment company Shock dose biocide — per treatment plan Temporarily isolate the tower if possible — alternative cooling Root cause: water temperature, low biocide, stagnant areas Retest before returning to service Regulatory reporting may be required Cooling Tower vs Air-Cooled Chiller Cooling Tower + Water-Cooled Chiller Air-Cooled Chiller (no tower) Best Practices Legionella management plan: Written plan, regular testing, documented treatment — it is also a legal requirement in many regions. VFD on all fans: 40-50% fan energy savings. ROI typically 2-3 years. Water treatment partner: Engage a specialist water treatment company — better expertise than in-house. N+1 tower cells: Ensure redundancy — a single cell failure should still keep the data center cool. Cycles of concentration optimization: Higher cycles = less water waste. But monitor TDS carefully. Drift eliminator maintenance: Regular inspect, replace before failure. Drift = water loss + Legionella risk. Basin sweep and clean: Sediment accumulates — a breeding ground for bacteria. headings: How CRAC Works Inside a Data Center
A CRAC is a self-contained cooling unit — it has its own compressor, pulls warm air in and pushes cool air out.
crac.bodyText: 🌬️ QUICK SUMMARY — 2 MINUTE READ Engineer's Tip Why This Matters In A Data Center On The Data Center Map KEY TAKEAWAYS Imagine a 500 sqm server room. Thousands of servers. Round-the-clock operation. All the servers are generating heat. This heat has to go somewhere. We read about the Computer Room Air Conditioner. The name itself tells you everything — an air conditioner made specifically for computer rooms (data centers). CRAC unit — floor-mounted, typically 0.5m to 1m wide, 1.8m tall. It is installed inside the server room alongside the racks. What Is a CRAC? CRAC = Computer Room Air Conditioner. It is a specialized, self-contained cooling unit designed for Data Centers and Computer Rooms. "Self-contained" means — its refrigeration system is within itself. The compressor is inside it or in a directly connected external unit. The job of a CRAC is simple: Pull warm air from the server racks Cool it with the refrigeration cycle Send the cool air back into the room Repeat — 24×7 There is a lot of confusion in the industry about CRAC and PAC. Technically, both use DX (Direct Expansion) cooling. Practically, the external condenser of a CRAC is usually more visible — on a wall or on the roof. In a PAC an all-in-one or close-coupled design is more common. But both are basically the same technology — same goal, similar operation. Why Is CRAC Needed? Servers do not waste electricity — they use electricity for computation. But every watt of electricity a server consumes is eventually converted into heat. This is a law of physics — there is no escape. A 1000W server = generates 1000W of heat. 20 racks × 10 kW average = 200 kW of heat. That is enough heat to warm a small house. According to ASHRAE thermal guidelines, server inlet temperature should be 18°C to 27°C (A1 class equipment). If this range is exceeded, servers throttle performance, generate errors, and a thermal shutdown can happen. The CRAC maintains this temperature range — no matter what the IT load is, no matter what the time of day. Why specifically a CRAC — why not a normal AC? Continuous operation: A CRAC is rated to run 24×7×365 High sensible heat ratio: Servers only raise temperature (not moisture) — a CRAC is optimized for this Precise control: ±1°C temperature and ±5% humidity precision High capacity per unit: 15-100+ kW per unit — a normal AC is 1-5 kW BMS integration: Centralized monitoring and alarm management Working Principle A CRAC uses the DX (Direct Expansion) refrigeration cycle "Direct Expansion" means the refrigerant expands directly in the evaporator coil. There is no intermediate water loop — the refrigerant transfers heat directly with the air. DX Cycle Step by Step Step 1 — Evaporator (inside, in the room): Low pressure liquid refrigerant comes into the evaporator coil. Warm air from the servers passes over this coil. The refrigerant absorbs the heat and turns into gas. The air gets cooled. Step 2 — Compressor: The low pressure refrigerant gas goes into the compressor. It is compressed to high pressure. Its temperature also rises. Step 3 — Condenser (outside, outside the building): The hot high-pressure gas goes into the outdoor condenser unit. Outdoor fans reject the heat into the ambient air. The gas turns into liquid. This heat effectively goes outside. Step 4 — Expansion Valve: The high pressure liquid passes through the expansion valve. The pressure drops suddenly. The refrigerant becomes cold. Then into the evaporator — cycle complete. Understand this fundamental difference between a DX system and a chilled water system: in DX, the refrigerant cools the air directly. In a chilled water system, the refrigerant first cools water, then that cool water cools the air in the CRAH. DX is simpler but has limited capacity. A chilled water system is complex but better for centralized cooling — that is why large data centers use chillers. Main Components Evaporator Coil: Air is cooled by the refrigerant here. Copper tubes + aluminum fins. Blower / Fan: Pulls and circulates the air. EC motors in modern units. Stops dust particles — protects the coil. Steam or electrode type — adds humidity when required. Electric Heater: Maintains temperature in cold weather. Microprocessor Controller: Temperature, humidity, alarms — controls everything. Condensate Pan + Drain: The water that comes out from dehumidification collects here. Outdoor Unit (Condenser) The heart of the refrigeration cycle — scroll or reciprocating type. Condenser Coil: Heat is rejected from the high pressure refrigerant gas. Condenser Fans: Reject heat into the outdoor air. Speed-controlled in modern units. Refrigerant Pipework: Connects the indoor and outdoor units — insulated copper pipes. Sight Glass: Visual check of refrigerant level and quality. Service Valves: Valves to isolate the refrigerant for maintenance. How CRAC Works Inside a Data Center CRAC unit airflow — return air in from the top, supply air from the bottom (through the raised floor via perforated tiles) or directly from the front. A CRAC unit is installed on the floor in the server room — typically at the end of the server racks or near a wall of the room. Downflow CRAC (Most Common) Warm return air comes in from the top of the unit. It is cooled by the evaporator coil. Cool supply air goes down — into the raised floor. It comes into the cold aisle through perforated floor tiles. Servers pull in the cool air. Warm exhaust air goes into the hot aisle — then returns to the CRAC. Cycle complete. Upflow CRAC (No Raised Floor) Warm return air enters from the bottom. Cool supply air comes out from the top. It is distributed at ceiling level or through overhead ducts. There is more mixing before it reaches the servers — slightly less efficient. CRAC unit placement is critical in a Data Center. Rule of thumb: one CRAC unit for every 5-7 racks. Distribute the units evenly in the room — do not put them in corners or on walls — cooling will stay uniform. Hot spots come only when cooling units are maldistributed. Types of CRAC 1. Air-Cooled CRAC The condenser rejects heat into the outdoor air. The external condenser unit is installed outside the building. The most common type. Simpler installation — no water supply needed. Efficiency drops at high ambient temperature. 2. Water-Cooled CRAC The condenser rejects heat into cooling water. Supply comes from a water chiller or cooling tower. Better efficiency than air-cooled — independent of ambient temperature. Water infrastructure is necessary. 3. Glycol-Cooled CRAC A water-cooled variant — uses a glycol-water mixture. For freeze protection — in cold climates. A dry cooler (fluid cooler) is installed outside — no evaporation, no refrigerant in the outdoor unit. 4. Chilled Water CRAC (CRAH) Technically this becomes a CRAH (Air Handler) when chilled water is used. No compressor inside the unit. Just fan + water coil. The chiller system provides the chilled water. Large data centers prefer this for scalability. Self-contained DX system: No chiller plant needed — simpler infrastructure Quick deployment: Install, charge refrigerant, commissioning — ready Precision cooling: Precise control of temperature and humidity Continuous duty rated: 24×7×365 operation Add units as load increases N+1 redundancy: Easy to achieve Disadvantages External condenser: A unit is needed outside the building — site constraints Ambient dependency: Cooling capacity reduces at high outdoor temperature Limited scalability: For very large data centers a chiller plant is more efficient Compressor maintenance: Moving parts — wear and tear, eventually replacement Refrigerant leak risk: Leaks are possible at piping connections The compressor and condenser fans generate noise Real Data Center Example A telecom company's 300 sqm server room. 30 racks, average 8 kW per rack = 240 kW total heat load. Cooling design: Air-cooled CRAC, 30 kW capacity per unit. 9 units required (270 kW) + 1 standby = 10 units total (N+1). 5 units each side of the room. Downflow units with raised floor 600mm height. 10 condenser units on the roof — each paired with an indoor CRAC unit. All units connected to BMS. Master/slave configuration — automatic standby rotation every 30 days. Common Faults High Supply Air Temperature Possible causes: Dirty filter, low refrigerant, high ambient temperature, compressor issue. Action: Check the filter, check refrigerant pressure, clean the condenser. Compressor Trip Possible causes: High head pressure, low suction pressure, overload, internal fault. Action: Confirm the standby unit is running → read the fault code → call a qualified technician. Condenser Fan Failure Possible causes: Motor fault, belt break (older units), blade damage. Effect: High head pressure → compressor trip. Action: Replace the fan. Refrigerant Leak Possible causes: Pipe joint wear, valve leak, coil damage. Signs: Low suction pressure, poor cooling, ice on the evaporator coil. Action: Detect the leak → repair → recharge — licensed technician only. Humidity Out of Range Possible causes: Humidifier failure, dehumidification issue, water supply. Action: Verify the humidity sensor, check humidifier status. Preventive Maintenance Quarterly PM Air filter clean / replace Inspect and clean the evaporator coil Clear the condensate drain Refrigerant pressure check — suction and discharge Measure superheat and subcooling Tighten electrical connections Check compressor current draw Verify controller settings Outdoor Condenser PM Clean the condenser coil — use a fin straightener Inspect the fan blades Fan motor current draw Check refrigerant pipe insulation Check weather proofing Daily Inspection Checklist ✓ Supply air temperature (target: 18-22°C) ✓ Return air temperature (target: 27-35°C) ✓ Room humidity (target: 40-60% RH) ✓ All units status — running / standby / fault ✓ BMS alarms — any active alarms? ✓ Outdoor condenser units — visually check (noise, vibration) ✓ Water leak check — condensate drain area ✓ Compressor running (sound check) ✓ Log book update Monthly Checklist ✓ Inspect the filter — clean or replace ✓ Condensate drain flush ✓ Switchover test — primary to standby transfer ✓ Temperature/humidity sensor calibration check ✓ BMS alarm log review ✓ Electrical panel check — breakers status ✓ Outdoor unit visual check — debris, clearance ✓ Record all readings in log Safety Precautions LOTO procedure: Electrical isolation is mandatory before maintenance Refrigerant handling: Certified technician only — direct exposure harmful High pressure hazard: Do not open the refrigerant system without authorization Outdoor unit safety: Maintain clearance while the condenser fan is running Working at height: Condenser maintenance on the roof — fall protection is essential Standby confirm: Confirm the standby unit is running before maintenance Gloves, safety glasses, proper footwear Interview Questions Q1: What is the difference between CRAC and CRAH? A CRAC has its own compressor and uses DX cooling — a self-contained unit. A CRAH has no compressor — it uses chilled water from outside (from the chiller plant). CRAC = complete unit. CRAH = just an air handler, the chiller is separate. Q2: How is CRAC unit sizing done? Calculate the IT load (in kW). For N+1 redundancy: N units handle the full load, 1 extra standby. Example: 100 kW load, 20 kW per unit → 5 units needed + 1 standby = 6 total. Running each unit at 80% load is best practice. Q3: What does a high head pressure alarm indicate? A condenser side problem. Possible causes: dirty condenser coil, condenser fan failure, high ambient temperature, refrigerant overcharge. The compressor can trip. Immediate action: check the condenser, verify fan status. Q4: What is superheat in a CRAC and why is it measured? Superheat = refrigerant gas temperature at the evaporator outlet minus the saturation temperature. Target: 6-12°C superheat. Low superheat → liquid refrigerant can enter the compressor (liquid slugging — dangerous). High superheat → low refrigerant or an expansion valve problem. It is a method to verify the refrigerant charge. Troubleshooting Guide Scenario: Room temperature is going above 28°C How many CRAC units are actually running? → All should be active Filter clog? → Differential pressure check Measure the supply air temperature → is cold air coming from the PAC? Hot/cold aisle mixing? → Check the blanking panels Was new IT equipment added? → Recalculate the heat load Outdoor ambient temperature → High ambient → derating effect Scenario: The compressor has tripped Immediately confirm the standby unit is running Read the controller fault code High head pressure alarm? → Check the condenser fan Low suction pressure? → Refrigerant leak suspect Overload trip? → Do an electrical check Call a qualified HVAC technician — do not DIY CRAC vs PAC vs CRAH Best Practices At least one standby unit — no downtime on failure Standby rotation: Regularly switch the primary and standby — equal wear Hot/cold aisle separation: CRAC cooling becomes 30-40% more efficient Filter maintenance schedule: Mark it on the calendar — do not skip it Setpoint consistency: Run all CRAC units at the same setpoint Outdoor condenser clearance: Minimum 1m clearance on all sides — do not block the airflow Monitor all units — manual rounds are not enough Annual refrigerant audit: Have the system checked by a licensed technician Key Takeaways Frequently Asked Questions Related Learning Topics CRAC is clear. headings: How PAC Works Inside a Data Center
A PAC is a precision cooling unit installed near the server racks in a Data Center that keeps them cool 24×7.
pac.bodyText: ❄️ QUICK SUMMARY — 2 MINUTE READ If you have understood this much, the PAC concept is clear. The full article is ahead — from working principle to troubleshooting. Engineer's Tip Why This Matters In A Data Center On The Data Center Map KEY TAKEAWAYS Imagine a bank's server room. There are only 20 servers. The room is small — 10×10 feet. Those 20 servers work 24 hours. At night too. On weekends too. 365 days a year. These servers generate heat. If this heat stays in the room, the temperature will climb to 45°C, 50°C, 60°C. If servers go above 35-40°C, they shut down. The solution to exactly this problem is — the PAC (Precision Air Conditioner). PAC unit — installed in a Data Center server room. This white/grey cabinet sits near the servers. What Is a PAC? PAC = Precision Air Conditioner. It is a specialized cooling unit designed specifically for Data Centers and Server Rooms. Compare it with a home AC: Home AC → to keep people comfortable. 22°C to 26°C. Switched off at night. PAC → to keep servers safe. 18°C to 24°C. Never switched off. A PAC does not only control temperature — it also controls humidity. Low humidity → static electricity → components can get damaged. High humidity → moisture → corrosion, short circuit. Ideal range: Temperature 18-27°C, Humidity 40-60% RH. Why Is PAC Needed? Servers consume electricity. This electricity turns into heat. A typical 1U server generates 200-400W. One rack can have 20-40 servers. Heat of one rack: 20 servers × 300W = 6000W = 6 kW. Heat of 20 racks: 20 × 6 kW = Where will this heat go? It has to be removed. Otherwise the room will become an oven. According to the standards of ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers), the server inlet temperature in a Data Center should be 18°C to 27°C. If this range is crossed, server performance degrades, component life span reduces, and a thermal shutdown can happen. A normal building AC does not work because: Continuous operation: A normal AC is designed for 8-12 hours. A PAC works 8760 hours/year (365 × 24). High heat density: Servers generate a lot of heat in a small space. A normal AC does not have the capacity for this. Humidity control: A normal AC only controls temperature. Not humidity. A normal AC accepts ±3-5°C variation. A PAC maintains ±1°C. Sensible heat ratio: Servers generate sensible heat (raises temperature, not moisture). A normal AC has a low SHR — it is built to cool humid air. Working Principle A PAC works on a simple principle: Warm air in → cool it → cool air out. This cycle is achieved using a refrigerant (a special gas). A PAC has a fan that pulls warm air from the server racks. This warm air passes through the evaporator coil, where the refrigerant is. The refrigerant absorbs this heat. Now cool air comes out through the fan and cools the servers. This cycle repeats continuously. Refrigeration Cycle Explained Understanding the refrigeration cycle is essential. Don't worry — it is simple. is a special fluid that can easily turn from liquid to gas and from gas to liquid. Cooling happens by using this property: Step 1 — Evaporator (Cooling Happens Here) The refrigerant comes into the evaporator coil in liquid form. Warm air passes over the coil. The refrigerant absorbs this heat and turns into gas. The air gets cooled. In a cooler, water evaporates and you feel cool — same concept. Step 2 — Compressor (Pressure Increase) The gas-form refrigerant goes into the compressor. The compressor compresses it to high pressure. Compression also raises its temperature — it is now a hot compressed gas. Step 3 — Condenser (Heat Release) The hot compressed gas goes into the condenser. Here it releases heat. The heat leaves through the condenser — outside the building or into a cooling tower. The gas turns into liquid. Step 4 — Expansion Valve (Pressure Drop) The liquid refrigerant passes through the expansion valve. The pressure drops. The refrigerant becomes cold. Now it goes back into the evaporator — cycle complete. A shortcut to remember the refrigeration cycle: Evaporator = absorb, Compressor = compress, Condenser = reject, Expansion = expand. ECCE — never forget this sequence. Main Components 1. Compressor The "heart" of the PAC. It compresses the refrigerant gas. It is the most power-consuming component. Modern units have a scroll type or reciprocating type. 2. Evaporator Coil (Indoor Coil) This is where the actual cooling happens. The refrigerant passes through this coil and absorbs the heat of the warm air. It is an assembly of fins and tubes — more surface area = more heat transfer. 3. Condenser It releases heat outside. It can be air-cooled (air via fan) or water-cooled (via chilled water). A self-contained PAC has an air-cooled condenser. 4. Expansion Valve (TEV / EEV) It controls the flow and pressure of the refrigerant. TEV = Thermostatic Expansion Valve (mechanical). EEV = Electronic Expansion Valve (electronic control — more precise). Modern PACs use an EEV. 5. Fan / Blower It pulls air from the server racks and returns cool air. Modern PACs have EC (Electronically Commutated) fans — their speed is variable and they are energy efficient. 6. Microprocessor Controller The "brain" of the PAC. It takes readings from temperature and humidity sensors. It controls the compressor, fans and heater. It generates alarms. It communicates with the BMS (Building Management System). 7. Humidifier / Dehumidifier For humidity control. If humidity is low, the humidifier adds steam or water mist. If humidity is high, moisture is removed through condensation in dehumidification mode. 8. Electric Heater (Optional) In cold weather, when there is not enough heat from the servers, the PAC can also do heating. This ensures the temperature does not go below the minimum. How PAC Works Inside a Data Center Now look at it in a real Data Center scenario. Cold Aisle / Hot Aisle arrangement — cool air from the PAC goes into the cold aisle, hot air collects in the hot aisle. In a Data Center, server racks are installed in rows. Between the racks there are two kinds of aisles (corridors): — where cold air comes from the PAC. The front side of the servers faces here. — where hot air comes out of the servers. The back side of the servers faces here. The PAC is installed in or near the cold aisle. Cool air goes into the cold aisle → passes through the servers → comes out into the hot aisle → the PAC pulls it back → cools it → then into the cold aisle again. This is a closed loop. One important point: cool air from a PAC can come from below or from above. In a raised floor system, the PAC sends cool air under the raised floor and it comes out through perforated tiles. This is what keeps the cold aisle cool. Without a raised floor, the PAC delivers cool air directly from floor level or from the ceiling. Types of PAC 1. Downflow PAC Cool air comes out from below — into the raised floor. The most common type. Warm air is pulled from the racks from above. 2. Upflow PAC Cool air comes out from above. When there is no raised floor. Air is distributed directly from ceiling level or through overhead ducts. 3. In-Row Cooling The PAC unit is installed directly between rack rows. Cooling very close to the heat load. Best for high-density environments. Short air paths — efficient. 4. In-Rack Cooling The cooling unit is installed directly inside the rack. For ultra-high density servers. Rare — mostly in specialized applications. 5. Air-Cooled PAC The condenser releases heat to the outside air. The external condenser is installed outside the building on a wall or on the roof. Simpler installation. 6. Water-Cooled PAC The condenser releases heat into a chilled water loop. It works with a chiller system. Better efficiency but requires water infrastructure. Precision control: Maintains temperature ±1°C, humidity ±5% RH 24×7 operation: Continuous duty rated — never switched off A perfect match for the server heat profile Self-contained: Compressor, condenser — all in one unit (in the air-cooled type) Redundancy possible: N+1 design — if one fails, another is active BMS integration: Remote monitoring and alarms Add new units as load increases Disadvantages Higher cost: 3-5x more expensive than a normal AC Space requirement: Large units take up floor space External condenser: The air-cooled type also needs an outdoor unit Energy consumption: Runs 24×7 — higher electricity bill Skilled maintenance: Needs an HVAC certified technician Limited for high density: Very high density racks (20+ kW/rack) need supplementary cooling Real Data Center Example A 200 sqm colocation data center, 50 racks, average 5 kW per rack. Total heat load: 50 × 5 = 250 kW 10 PAC units of 30 kW cooling capacity (total 300 kW) — in N+1, 9 units are enough, 1 standby. Arrangement: Downflow PAC, raised floor 500mm height. Cold aisle / hot aisle containment. N+1 — if any one unit fails, the remaining 9 will handle the full load. All PACs are connected to the BMS. Temperature, humidity, alarms — everything is monitored centrally. In real data centers, PAC units are checked 24×7. The BMS has a dedicated cooling overview screen showing each PAC's status, temperature readings and alarms. If any PAC gives a high temperature alarm, it is investigated immediately — nobody waits. Common Faults 1. High Supply Air Temperature Alarm Dirty filters, low refrigerant, compressor issue, high room heat load. Server inlet temperature rises. A high temperature alarm is triggered. 2. High/Low Humidity Alarm Humidifier failure, dehumidification circuit issue, water supply problem. Static discharge risk (low humidity), condensation risk (high humidity). 3. High Head Pressure Dirty condenser coil, condenser fan failure, refrigerant overcharge, high outdoor temperature. The compressor trips, cooling stops. 4. Low Suction Pressure (Low Refrigerant) Refrigerant leak, expansion valve issue. Cooling capacity reduces, the evaporator can freeze. 5. Filter Clog Alarm Air filters have clogged — dust, particles. Airflow reduces, cooling efficiency drops. 6. Water Leak / Condensate Drain Block Drain pan full, drain pipe blocked. Water leak → equipment damage → serious hazard. Preventive Maintenance Quarterly (3 months) maintenance: Clean or replace the air filter Inspect the evaporator coil — clean the fins Clean the condenser coil Check refrigerant pressure (suction and discharge) Tighten electrical connections Check fan belts or bearings (older units) Clean the condensate drain Verify controller settings Check temperature calibration Annual maintenance: Full refrigerant system check — leak test Verify compressor current draw Recalibrate all sensors Replace the humidifier cylinder (if applicable) Electrical insulation test Daily Inspection Checklist ✓ Note the supply air temperature reading (target 18-22°C) ✓ Return air temperature reading (target 27-35°C) ✓ Room humidity reading (target 40-60% RH) ✓ PAC unit status — running / standby / fault ✓ Check active alarms — on the BMS ✓ Check for unusual noise or vibration ✓ Check for water leaks — drain pan area ✓ Filter differential pressure (if monitored) ✓ Compressor running status ✓ Fan status — speed and airflow Monthly Checklist ✓ Inspect the air filter — does it need cleaning or replacing? ✓ Flush the condensate drain — check for blockage ✓ Visually inspect the evaporator coil ✓ Verify temperature/humidity sensor readings — are they calibrated? ✓ Do a PAC switchover test — start the standby unit, stop the primary — does it transfer smoothly? ✓ Review BMS alarm history — identify recurring issues ✓ Electrical panel — check breakers and switches ✓ Update the log book — readings, maintenance done Safety Precautions Electrical isolation: Before maintenance, switch off the MCB/MCCB and apply LOTO (Lockout Tagout) Refrigerant handling: Only a certified HVAC technician should handle refrigerant — direct skin contact or inhalation is dangerous High pressure: The refrigerant system is under high pressure — unauthorized opening is dangerous Water leak response: As soon as a leak is seen, clear it away from electrical equipment — it is also a slip hazard Gloves and safety glasses are mandatory — during maintenance Permit to Work: It is not hot work, but an entry permit and LOTO are mandatory — follow the data center policy Ensure redundancy: Before maintenance, confirm that the standby unit is running Interview Questions Q1: What is the difference between a PAC and a normal AC? A PAC is for precision cooling — continuous duty, humidity control, high SHR. A normal AC is for human comfort — intermittent use, only temperature control, low SHR. A PAC maintains server inlet temperature within ±1°C. Q2: What is SHR and why is it important in a Data Center? SHR = Sensible Heat Ratio = Sensible cooling / Total cooling. Servers generate only sensible heat (temperature), not latent heat (moisture). A PAC's SHR should be 0.90-0.95 — this matches the load profile of servers. A normal AC's SHR is 0.65-0.75 — it is designed for humid air. Q3: What is N+1 redundancy in the context of a PAC? N = required units, +1 = one extra unit. If 9 units are enough to run the full load, install 10. If one fails, the remaining 9 handle the load. No downtime. Q4: What does a high head pressure alarm in a PAC indicate? A problem on the condenser side — dirty condenser coil, condenser fan failure, high ambient temperature, or refrigerant overcharge. The compressor can trip — immediate investigation is necessary. Q5: What is a cold aisle / hot aisle? Server racks are installed facing alternate directions. In the cold aisle, the fronts of the servers face — cool air from the PAC comes here. In the hot aisle, the backs of the servers — exhaust air comes out here. Mixing reduces and cooling efficiency improves. Troubleshooting Guide Problem: Room temperature is rising Check: How many PAC units are actually running? Check the filter — is it clogged? Measure the supply air temperature — is cool air coming from the PAC? Check hot aisle / cold aisle separation — is mixing happening? Has the IT load suddenly increased — were new servers added? Problem: Humidity out of range Check the humidity reading on the PAC controller Check humidifier status — is there a fault alarm? Check the water supply to the humidifier Compare readings of multiple PACs — single unit issue or systemic? Problem: PAC has tripped / fault alarm Read the fault code on the controller display Immediately confirm the standby unit is running Check for an MCB/circuit breaker trip High head pressure → check the condenser Low suction pressure → suspect a refrigerant leak → call a qualified technician PAC vs Normal AC Best Practices Never keep a single point of failure. There should be at least one extra PAC. Hot/Cold aisle containment: PAC efficiency improves by 30-40% with containment. Blanking panels: Install blanking panels in empty rack spaces — it stops hot/cold air mixing. Filter schedule: Regular filter maintenance = consistent airflow = consistent cooling. Setpoint management: Keep the room temperature setpoint at 21-23°C — colder is a waste of energy. Connect all PACs to the BMS — remote monitoring and automatic alarms. Standby rotation: Rotate the primary and standby units — equal wear on both. Load balancing: Distribute PAC units evenly in the room — avoid hot spots. Key Takeaways Frequently Asked Questions Related Learning Topics Now the PAC is clear. Understand the cooling system further: — the PAC's cousin. Different compressor approach, same goal. — the centralized cooling system in large data centers. — Hot aisle / cold aisle containment — improves PAC efficiency. — how cool air reaches the right place — complete guide. — a metric to measure cooling effectiveness. What is a PAC, how does it work, why is it used in a Data Center — working principle, components, types, maintenance and troubleshooting. In simple English. The first step of Data Center cooling — how a PAC works, where it is installed, and why it is different from a normal AC. Precision Air Conditioner — the basic unit of Data Center cooling, in simple language. 1px solid rgba(37,99,235,0.08) A PAC is a precision cooling unit installed near the server racks in a Data Center that keeps them cool 24×7. Why it is different from a normal AC A home AC only controls temperature. A PAC controls both temperature and humidity, runs non-stop, and delivers safe cool air for servers. Compressor, evaporator coil, condenser, expansion valve — together they run the refrigeration cycle. Warm air comes in, cool air goes out. Where in a Data Center Inside the server room, beside the racks or at the end of a row. It is mounted directly on the floor or on a raised floor. How important it is Without cooling, servers overheat in 10-15 minutes. The PAC prevents this failure — it is a critical infrastructure component. Difference from CRAC A PAC is self-contained — it has its own compressor, condenser, everything. A CRAC has a chilled water system or an external condenser. Both do the same job — the approach is different. From Server Racks Evaporator Coil Liquid → Gas, Heat absorb Gas gets compressed Gas → Liquid, Heat release Expansion Valve

faqs.q: What is the difference between a PAC and a normal AC?
faqs.a: A normal AC only controls temperature and is designed for human comfort. A PAC controls both temperature and humidity, is built for 24×7 continuous operation, and delivers precise airflow for servers. A normal AC does not have this much precision.

faqs.q: What is the kW rating of a PAC?
faqs.a: Typically from 5 kW to 60 kW. Small server rooms use 10-20 kW units. In large data centers, multiple units work in parallel.

faqs.q: How often should a PAC be serviced?
faqs.a: Daily inspection, monthly filter cleaning, and quarterly full preventive maintenance. If the cooling load is high, more frequent servicing is necessary.

faqs.q: What happens if a PAC fails?
faqs.a: The redundant PAC will automatically take the load (in an N+1 design). The IT equipment will trigger a temperature alarm. If cooling fails completely, servers will shut down. That is why redundancy is essential.

faqs.q: Which refrigerant is used in a PAC?
faqs.a: Mostly R410A or R407C in modern units. Older units had R22, which is now being phased out. The refrigerant type is written on the unit

faqs.q: What is the SHR of a PAC?
faqs.a: SHR = Sensible Heat Ratio. In a Data Center, servers generate only sensible heat (they raise temperature); latent heat (moisture) is low. The SHR of a PAC is 0.90-0.95 — a perfect match for the heat profile of servers.

RCI in a Real Data Center
RCI > 91% = Excellent. 81–90% = Good. 71–80% = Fair. < 70% = Poor — immediate action needed.
rci.bodyText: 91% = Excellent. 81–90% = Good. 71–80% = Fair. 📊 QUICK SUMMARY — 2 MINUTE READ If you have understood this much, the RCI concept is clear. The full article ahead has the calculation, examples and troubleshooting. Engineer's Tip Why This Matters In A Data Center On The Data Center Map KEY TAKEAWAYS What It Means 91% means the PAC/CRAC is getting proper hot return air — bypass air is low. Low RHI ( Imagine a Data Center with 200 racks. The PAC units are running. The cooling system is running. But the CPU temperature of some servers is going above 75°C — alarms are coming. Some servers are throttling — performance is dropping. What is the problem? The cooling system is running. It does not matter just that the cooling system runs — what matters is whether the cooling is being delivered to the right place, at the right temperature. The answer to this question comes from — RCI (Rack Cooling Index). RCI is a metric — a number — that tells how effective the cooling delivery is. RCI measurement — collect data from every rack's inlet temperature sensor. These numbers are used to calculate RCI. What Is RCI? RCI = Rack Cooling Index. It is a percentage metric — from 0% to 100% — that measures how many servers in the Data Center are getting cool air within the recommended temperature range. ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) defined this metric. The ASHRAE TC 9.9 committee maintains the Data Center thermal management standards. RCI 100% = Perfect. Every server's inlet temperature is within the ASHRAE recommended range. RCI 0% = Catastrophic. No server is within the recommended range. In real data centers the target is RCI > 91%. RCI does not only track over-heating — it also detects over-cooling. If servers are much too cold (below 18°C), that is also energy waste — the cooling is running more than needed. RCI penalises both extremes — going outside the perfect range costs points in the score. Why Is RCI Needed? Confirming that a PAC unit is running in the Data Center is not enough. It is essential to confirm that: Every rack is getting adequate cool air No rack is in an overheating zone Cool air is not being wasted (over-cooling) Cooling improvement actions are having an actual effect Without RCI, data center operators manage cooling by "feel" — they find out there is a problem when a server alarm comes. RCI is proactive — you find out that cooling is deteriorating before servers alarm. After an RCI survey, fix the blanking panels, floor tiles, containment gaps — everything. Result: server reliability improves, energy cost reduces. Practical example: A new rack was installed. No alarm came. But RCI dropped from 88% to 79%. Some older racks are now taking in warm air. Without RCI this was invisible. How RCI Is Calculated To calculate RCI you need just one thing: the inlet temperature of every rack. Inlet temperature = at the front face of the server, at the bottom of the rack (or at multiple points) — this is where cool air enters. ASHRAE has defined temperature ranges: Recommended range: 18°C – 27°C (ideal for most servers) Allowable range (upper): 27°C – 35°C (varies according to equipment specs) Below recommended: < 18°C (over-cooling — energy waste) Above allowable: > 35°C (equipment damage zone) The RCI formula measures these deviations and expresses them as a single percentage. RCI Formula Step by Step RCI has two parts: — High side: racks that are hotter than recommended — Low side: racks that are colder than recommended Both are calculated separately, then a combined score is obtained. RCI(HI) — Over-Temperature Penalty For every rack, check: is the inlet temperature above 27°C? calculate the deviation: Deviation = Actual temperature − T_recommended_max (27°C) Sum this deviation for all racks. RCI(HI) = 1 − [Σ(T_measured − T_rec_max) / Σ(T_allowable_max − T_rec_max)] × 100% When a rack is within the recommended range — its deviation = 0 (no penalty). When all racks are within the recommended range — total deviation = 0, RCI(HI) = 100%. RCI(LO) — Under-Temperature Penalty Same concept — but on the lower side. Is the inlet temperature below 18°C? Deviation = T_recommended_min (18°C) − Actual temperature RCI(LO) = 1 − [Σ(T_rec_min − T_measured) / Σ(T_rec_min − T_allowable_min)] × 100% In the field a simplified approach is common: measure all rack inlets, count how many are within 18–27°C. Rough RCI ≈ (in-range racks / total racks) × 100. This is not the exact ASHRAE formula — but it is useful for a quick assessment. For a proper RCI, use DCIM software or a detailed spreadsheet. RHI — Return Heat Index Along with RCI, RHI (Return Heat Index) is usually also measured. RHI measures how much hot return air the PAC/CRAC unit is getting back — relative to what it should be getting. Simple explanation: High RHI (> 91%) = actual hot air is returning to the PAC — the servers' heat is being captured effectively. Good. Low RHI (< 80%) = cool air is bypassing — it is going back into the PAC without reaching the servers. Cooling wasted. RCI and RHI together give the full picture: RCI high + RHI high = Perfect cooling delivery RCI low + RHI high = Servers are hot but heat is captured — cooling is insufficient RCI high + RHI low = Cool air is wasted, it is bypassing RCI low + RHI low = Multiple problems — immediate action Practical use of RHI: if RHI is 70%, it means 30% of the cool air is bypassing — it is coming back to the PAC without reaching the servers. The reasons for this 30% energy waste: wrong floor tile placement, gaps under racks, perforated tiles directly in front of the PAC. Fix these — RHI will improve, energy will be saved, and that cool air will actually reach the servers. What You Need to Measure RCI 1. Temperature Sensors Install a temperature sensor at every rack's inlet. Minimum: one sensor at 1U height (bottom of the rack). Better: 3 points — bottom (1U), middle, top. Temperature can vary at different heights. Sensor types: wired thermocouple or RTD sensors connected to the DCIM system. Wireless sensors are available — easier for retrofit. Some intelligent PDUs also have built-in sensors. 2. DCIM Software (Recommended) Data Center Infrastructure Management software — automatically collects sensor data, calculates RCI/RHI, maintains historical trending and generates alerts. Popular DCIM tools: EkkoSense, Nlyte, Sunbird, Vertiv Avocent. Essential for large data centers. 3. Spreadsheet (Manual Approach) In small data centers: measure the temperature manually at every rack. Enter it in a spreadsheet. Apply the formula. Quarterly or semi-annually is useful for establishing a baseline. 4. IR Thermometer / Thermal Camera For quick spot checks. An instantaneous reading at the rack inlet with an IR thermometer. With a thermal camera you can visually see a temperature map of the entire aisle. Hot spots are immediately visible. RCI in a Real Data Center RCI heat map — generated by DCIM software. Blue = cold (over-cooling), green = ideal, yellow/red = hot spots. How RCI works in daily operations: DCIM software collects the temperature from every sensor every 5 minutes. The software automatically calculates RCI and RHI — per row, per zone and at the overall facility level. The dashboard shows a color-coded heatmap — which racks are in the ideal range, which are borderline, which are problematic. If any zone goes below 80% — an automatic alert is generated. The operations team investigates. Implement the fix (blanking panels, tile replacement, PAC adjustment). The RCI trend improves — it is verified that the fix worked. Field tip: Whenever you install a new rack, immediately check the RCI around it. New rack = new heat load = existing cooling distribution can be affected. Before installation: note the RCI baseline. After installation: check again. If there is a dip — address it before it becomes a problem. RCI Score Ranges ASHRAE TC 9.9 has defined these rating tiers for RCI: Industry target: RCI consistently > 91%. Maintaining 91%+ is expected in Tier III and Tier IV certified facilities. Why RCI Is Useful Objective measurement: Better than "cooling seems fine" — RCI = an actual number Detect a cooling problem before a server alarm Baseline comparison: Compare before/after changes — prove the improvement Hotspot identification: Exactly which rack, which row — pinpoint it Catch over-cooling: Identify energy waste — optimize PAC setpoints Capacity planning: Before increasing load — check the current RCI. Is there a buffer? SLA compliance: Prove to clients that cooling is adequate Justify cooling investment: Low RCI → a concrete reason for cooling upgrades Limitations of RCI Sensors needed: RCI cannot be calculated without temperature sensors. You have to invest in infrastructure. Snapshot metric: RCI is a point-in-time measurement. Load constantly changes — a single measurement does not give the full picture. RCI measures server inlet temperature — not the temperature inside the server. Airflow within the server is also important. ASHRAE Class assumptions: There are different acceptable ranges for different equipment classes. A single RCI calculation does not always capture the differences of all equipment. Not a standalone metric: RCI can be high while PUE is poor — look at both together. Real Calculation Example 10 racks, temperature measured at each rack inlet. ASHRAE recommended range: 18°C – 27°C. Inlet Temp (°C) Deviation from Range 7 racks in recommended range (21, 23, 20, 22, 19, 24, 25°C) 2 racks over-temperature (29°C → +2°C, 31°C → +4°C) — total HI deviation = 6°C 1 rack under-temperature (15°C → −3°C) — LO deviation = 3°C Simplified RCI estimate: 7 of 10 racks in range = 70% — Fair category. R-06 (31°C) = highest priority. Check blanking panels in that rack. Check floor tile coverage. R-09 (15°C) = over-cooling, floor tile adjustment needed. R-04 (29°C) = monitor, check blanking panels. Common Causes of Poor RCI Missing Blanking Panels The most common cause. Hot exhaust air goes back into the server intake through an empty rack space — recirculation. The specific rack's RCI drops. Walk every rack, install blanking panels in every empty 1U/2U space. Immediate improvement milegi. Wrong Floor Tile Placement Perforated tiles are installed in the hot aisle or in front of the PAC — cool air is bypassing. There are no tiles in the cold aisle — cool air is not reaching. Floor tile audit. Perforated tiles only in the cold aisle, directly in front of the rack. No Containment or Containment Breach Containment is missing or damaged — hot/cold mixing. The RCI of the entire zone is affected. Implement or repair containment. Even a partial containment improvement is significant. Insufficient Cooling Capacity The IT load has increased — the cooling units are not enough. The RCI of the entire data center drops. Capacity planning. Additional PAC/CRAC units or chiller capacity. PAC/CRAC Placement Issues The cooling units are far from the racks where cooling is needed. Cold air is not reaching — the far racks' RCI is low. Add in-row cooling units in high-density areas. Optimize PAC placement. High Density Racks Without Supplementary Cooling For 10+ kW racks, standard PAC cooling can be insufficient. In-row cooling, rear-door heat exchangers or targeted supplementary cooling. How to Maintain Good RCI Maintaining RCI is an ongoing discipline — not a one-time fix. Physical Actions Verify blanking panels after every rack installation — always Audit floor tiles quarterly — confirm correct placement Check containment integrity monthly Keep PAC/CRAC filter maintenance regular — dirty filters = reduced airflow = RCI drop Cable management — manage cable bundles that block airflow Monitoring Actions Configure DCIM alerts — immediate alert if RCI goes below 85% Track temperature trends — so gradual deterioration is caught early Note seasonal changes — in summer outdoor temperature rises, chiller load rises, RCI impact is possible Quarterly full temperature mapping — all racks Daily Checklist ✓ Check the DCIM dashboard — current RCI score ✓ Is any RCI alert active? Investigate it ✓ Hot spot alarms — in the BMS or DCIM ✓ Cold aisle temperature — is it uniform? ✓ PAC/CRAC units all running? Any fault? ✓ New rack installed today? — Verify blanking panels and tiles ✓ RCI trend — improving, stable or deteriorating? Monthly Checklist ✓ Full temperature mapping — measure all rack inlets ✓ Calculate RCI and RHI (or generate the DCIM report) ✓ Comparison with the previous month — identify the trend ✓ Blanking panels walk — every rack row ✓ Floor tile placement audit ✓ Containment integrity check ✓ PAC/CRAC filter status — is the PM schedule current? ✓ Hot spots resolved? — Previous actions ne RCI improve kiya? ✓ Capacity vs IT load review — is the buffer adequate? Safety Notes Hot aisle temperature measurement: The hot aisle can reach 35–45°C. Use an IR thermometer from outside — avoid prolonged exposure. Raised floor access: Handle floor tiles carefully when installing temperature sensors in the raised floor. Heavy tiles — proper lifting technique. Working near live racks: During temperature measurement, keep hands and tools clear of rack equipment — avoid accidental contact. Thermal camera: Eye safety — avoid a direct IR flash. There is generally no risk with the camera, but follow standard PPE. Interview Questions Q1: What is RCI and what should its target be? RCI = Rack Cooling Index — a percentage metric that measures how many server racks are getting cool air within the ASHRAE recommended temperature range (18–27°C). Target: > 91% = Excellent. 81–90% = Good. Below 70% = Immediate action needed. 100% = every rack in range = perfect cooling delivery. Q2: RCI is low — what will you check first? Step 1: Look at the temperature heatmap — which racks/zones are affected. Step 2: Check blanking panels in the affected racks. Step 3: Verify the cold aisle floor tiles — are they perforated? Step 4: Is containment intact? Step 5: Are all PAC/CRAC units running, setpoints correct? Step 6: Recent changes — were new racks added? Q3: What is RHI and what does a low RHI mean? RHI = Return Heat Index — measures how much actual hot return air the PAC/CRAC is getting. Low RHI (<80%) = a bypass air problem — cool air is avoiding the servers and returning to the PAC. Causes: wrong floor tiles (perforated in front of the PAC), gaps in the raised floor, no containment. Fix: correct the tile placement, seal the gaps. Q4: What is the relationship between RCI and PUE? PUE = energy efficiency metric (total power / IT power). RCI = cooling quality metric (cooling delivery effectiveness). These two measure different things — both are essential. A good PUE with a poor RCI is possible — the cooling is energy efficient but is not being delivered to the right place. Target: PUE <1.4 AND RCI >91%. Q5: How can RCI be measured without DCIM? Manual approach: measure the temperature at every rack inlet with an IR thermometer (1U height). Enter it in a spreadsheet. Compare with the ASHRAE range (18–27°C). Count how many are in range. Simplified RCI % = (in-range racks / total racks) × 100. It is enough for a quarterly survey. Invest in DCIM for large facilities — manual is infeasible with hundreds of racks. Troubleshooting Guide Scenario: Overall RCI suddenly dropped — from 90% to 72% Look at the heatmap — is a specific zone affected or the full DC? Did something new happen? — New racks installed, a PAC unit down, a layout change? Check PAC/CRAC status — is any unit in fault? Outdoor temperature spike? — Seasonal load? Chiller capacity impacted? Check the blanking panels — were panels missed with new installations? Scenario: A specific row has low RCI every time Measure the cold aisle temperature of the affected row — is adequate cool air coming? Check the floor tiles in that row Distance to the nearest PAC unit — too far? Consider in-row cooling Is the rack density high in the row? — 8+ kW racks need supplementary cooling Is containment proper in that row? Scenario: RHI consistently low (bypass air problem) Floor tile placement audit — perforated tiles directly in front of the PAC? Raised floor gaps — cable openings sealed? Under-rack gaps — install sealing strips Are the containment end doors closed? PAC supply setpoints — too low? Raise them, bypass will reduce RCI vs PUE vs RHI 91% (High is good)", otherLabel: " Best Practices Measure first: An improvement cannot be proven without measurement. Establish a baseline RCI before any changes. Blanking panels 100% always: This is the most direct lever for RCI. Every rack, every empty space. No exceptions. Temperature sensors every rack: Bare minimum — bottom (1U) sensor. Better — 3-point measurement. Best — DCIM integration with real-time monitoring. Set alert thresholds: Set an 85% alert in DCIM — before things get critical. React before server alarms come. Include RCI in change management: An RCI check is mandatory after a new rack is installed. Document it. Trend monthly: A trend is more useful than a single data point. Know whether it is improving or deteriorating. Look at RCI + RHI together: Together they give the full cooling health picture. One metric is only half the story. Maintain a seasonal baseline: In summer RCI can naturally be slightly lower — understand what the normal range is. All these topics together have given the full cooling picture: — the primary method to improve RCI — optimize airflow. — hot/cold aisle containment — the most effective lever for RCI. — PAC and CRAC — which deliver the cool air that RCI measures. — the large data center cooling system — RCI is measured through the CRAH. — the heat rejection component of the chiller cooling chain. What is RCI, how is it calculated, what is a good RCI — the Rack Cooling Index is the metric of Data Center cooling effectiveness. A complete guide in simple English. RCI and RHI — the report card of Data Center cooling. How it is calculated, what a good score is, and how to improve it. Rack Cooling Index — the metric of Data Center cooling effectiveness. Complete guide. 1px solid rgba(37,99,235,0.08) RCI is a number — from 0% to 100% — that tells how much of the cool air servers in a Data Center are getting is within the right temperature range. What 100% means All servers are outside the recommended range — either too hot or too cold (over-cooling). The cooling system is not working properly. What the target should be RCI > 91% = Excellent. 81–90% = Good. 71–80% = Fair. < 70% = Poor — immediate action needed.
